description: The push-up is a bodyweight upper-body pressing movement that works the pectoral muscles, anterior deltoids, and triceps while simultaneously demanding core stability throughout. It is one of the most functional and scalable exercises — but it is commonly done with terrible form. The body must remain a rigid plank from head to heels for every single rep.
cues: Set your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width and angle fingers slightly outward
Before you move an inch — brace your abs as if you're about to take a punch
Squeeze your glutes so tight you could crack a walnut
Lower your chest — not your stomach, not your hips — your chest to the floor
Think about pulling the floor apart with your hands as you push up
Your elbows should point back and slightly out — not flaring out at 90 degrees
rules: Maintain a straight body line from head to heels throughout
Keep core engaged and hips level at all times
Lower chest until it nearly touches the ground
Keep elbows at 30 to 45 degrees relative to torso
Keep neck neutral — do not crane forward or drop the chin
constraints: Do not let hips sag toward the floor
Do not raise hips too high into a pike position
Avoid flaring elbows out to 90 degrees — strains the shoulder
Do not perform partial reps — chest must touch or nearly touch the floor
Maintain left-right symmetry — do not twist

hip_sagging.cause: Weak core, weak glutes, or fatigue causing loss of the rigid plank position.
hip_sagging.consequence: Compresses the lumbar spine significantly. Also eliminates core and hip involvement — making it effectively a half-rep.
hip_sagging.fix: Squeeze your glutes and draw your belly button to your spine before and during every rep. If you cannot hold the plank, drop to your knees.

hips_high.cause: Attempting to avoid hip sag by over-correcting — or tight pectoral muscles forcing the body forward.
hips_high.consequence: Shifts load off the chest onto the shoulders. It is essentially a partial downward-dog movement, not a push-up.
hips_high.fix: Visualise your body as a steel plank. Lower the hips until the body is a straight diagonal line from head to heels.

elbow_flare.cause: Hand placement too wide, or lack of awareness of ideal elbow path.
elbow_flare.consequence: Places the shoulder joint in internal rotation under load — a very common cause of rotator cuff injuries.
elbow_flare.fix: Bring hands in slightly and think about pointing your elbows back toward your hips as you lower. The angle to your torso should be roughly 45 degrees.

shallow_depth.cause: Fatigue, inadequate strength, or a habit of stopping early to get more reps.
shallow_depth.consequence: Partial reps only train a fraction of the muscle through its range — progress will plateau and strength will be uneven.
shallow_depth.fix: Do fewer reps fully than more reps shallowly. Chest should hover one inch from the floor at the bottom.

using_momentum.cause: Rushing reps or using a body bounce at the bottom to make the push-up easier.
using_momentum.consequence: Unloads the working muscles at the critical bottom position and adds jarring stress to the joints.
using_momentum.fix: Use a 2-second descent, one-second pause at the bottom, then a strong push up. Quality massively over quantity.

uneven_push.cause: Left-right strength imbalance or asymmetric hand placement.
uneven_push.consequence: Develops a muscular imbalance and can create a rotational stress on the spine or shoulder over time.
uneven_push.fix: Check hand placement is symmetrical. Do single-arm push-up negatives on the weaker side to correct the deficit.

tilt.note: Body tilt — should be nearly zero in a flat plank position

acceleration.note: Minimal vertical acceleration — controlled rep, no bounce

gyro.note: Rotation — left-right twist should be absent

stability.note: High stability expected during a ground-contact exercise

symmetry.note: Left and right arm loading should be equal
